claim: Complex motor skills take considerable time and practice to learn.
source: Complex motor skills take considerable time and practice to learn.
evidence: This is a general statement about motor learning presented as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Without continued practice the level of skill performance quickly degrades.
source: Without continued practice the level of skill performance quickly degrades, posing a problem for the timely utilization of skilled motor behaviors.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about motor skill maintenance.

claim: A songbird with prior singing experience can significantly accelerate the re-acquisition of vocal performance.
source: We demonstrate that a songbird with prior singing experience can significantly accelerate the re-acquisition of vocal performance.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data presented in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: An increase in vocal performance is accompanied by a pronounced synaptic pruning in the forebrain vocal motor area HVC.
source: We further demonstrate that an increase in vocal performance is accompanied by a pronounced synaptic pruning in the forebrain vocal motor area HVC, a reduction that is not reversed when birds stop singing.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5.

claim: The synaptic reduction in HVC is not reversed when birds stop singing.
source: We further demonstrate that an increase in vocal performance is accompanied by a pronounced synaptic pruning in the forebrain vocal motor area HVC, a reduction that is not reversed when birds stop singing.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 5 showing maintained low spine density in T1- group.

claim: Lasting synaptic changes in the motor circuitry are associated with the savings of motor skills.
source: These results provide evidence that lasting synaptic changes in the motor circuitry are associated with the savings of motor skills, enabling a rapid recovery of motor performance under environmental time constraints.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings combining the behavioral and anatomical data.

claim: Trained human surgeons need to re-acquire their surgical proficiency after a period of absence.
source: For example, trained human surgeons need to re-acquire their surgical proficiency after a period of absence (Crewther et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Crewther et al., 2016.

claim: Capuchin monkeys need to acquire manipulative foraging skills to retrieve difficult-to-access, seasonally available food items.
source: Capuchin monkeys need to acquire manipulative foraging skills to retrieve difficult-to-access, seasonally available food items (Eadie, 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Eadie, 2015.

claim: Songbirds need to re-develop high-quality songs to attract a mate after wintering or long-distance migration.
source: songbirds need to re-develop high-quality songs to attract a mate after wintering or long-distance migration (Slagsvold, 1976)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Slagsvold, 1976.

claim: Birdsong is an established model system for vocal motor learning.
source: Birdsong, an established model system for vocal motor learning (Brainard and Doupe, 2013)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Brainard and Doupe, 2013.

claim: Birdsong is characterized by a high degree of complex and rapid acoustic modulations.
source: Birdsong, an established model system for vocal motor learning (Brainard and Doupe, 2013), is characterized by a high degree of complex and rapid acoustic modulations.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about birdsong characteristics.

claim: The fine motor skills necessary to produce complex, high quality vocalizations are thought to advertise an individual's quality through performance-related characteristics.
source: The fine motor skills that are necessary to produce such complex, high quality vocalizations are thought to advertise an individual's quality through performance-related characteristics such as song complexity and/or production rate (Podos, 1997; Drăgănoiu et al., 2002; Holveck and Riebel, 2007; Byers et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Juvenile songbirds start singing noisy, unstructured 'subsongs' when they are one to two months old.
source: When juvenile songbirds are one to two months old they start singing noisy, unstructured 'subsongs' akin to human babbling (Doupe and Kuhl, 1999)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Doupe and Kuhl, 1999.

claim: Subsongs gradually develop into variable, but recognizable species-specific 'plastic songs'.
source: which gradually develop into variable, but recognizable species-specific 'plastic songs' (Marler and Peters, 1982a; Nottebohm et al., 1986; Tchernichovski et al., 2001; Mori et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: With extensive vocal rehearsal the songs slowly consolidate into high performance 'crystallized songs'.
source: With extensive vocal rehearsal the songs slowly consolidate into high performance 'crystallized songs', a process that can take up more than five months in some songbird species (Nottebohm et al., 1986).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Nottebohm et al., 1986.

claim: Song crystallization can take up more than five months in some songbird species.
source: With extensive vocal rehearsal the songs slowly consolidate into high performance 'crystallized songs', a process that can take up more than five months in some songbird species (Nottebohm et al., 1986).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Nottebohm et al., 1986.

claim: The seasonal development and degradation in vocal performance are highly correlated with changes in testosterone levels.
source: The seasonal development and degradation in vocal performance are highly correlated with changes in testosterone levels (Nottebohm et al., 1987; Smith et al., 1997; Tramontin et al., 2000; Voigt and Leitner, 2008)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Seasonal changes in vocal performance are often accompanied by gross anatomical and cytoarchitectural restructuring of the brain areas involved in song production.
source: and are often accompanied by gross anatomical and cytoarchitectural restructuring of the brain areas involved in song production (Nottebohm, 1981; Gahr, 1990; Kirn et al., 1994; Kafitz et al., 1999; Thompson and Brenowitz, 2005; Balthazart et al., 2008; Vellema et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Female canaries rarely sing spontaneously under natural conditions.
source: Although female canaries rarely sing spontaneously, and never produce high quality songs under natural conditions (Pesch and Guttinger, 1985)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pesch and Guttinger, 1985.

claim: Female canaries never produce high quality songs under natural conditions.
source: Although female canaries rarely sing spontaneously, and never produce high quality songs under natural conditions (Pesch and Guttinger, 1985)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pesch and Guttinger, 1985.

claim: The systemic application of testosterone leads to the development of high-performance song with male-typical features in female canaries.
source: the systemic application of testosterone leads to the development of high-performance song with male-typical features (Leonard, 1939; Shoemaker, 1939; Vallet et al., 1996)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Adult female canaries gradually develop stable, species-typical songs through a process of song crystallization during protracted testosterone treatment.
source: Here we demonstrate that during a protracted testosterone treatment, adult female canaries gradually develop stable, species-typical songs through a process of song crystallization similar to what is known for naturally-raised juvenile male canaries (Mori et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figure 1 and comparison to cited literature.

claim: Re-treatment with testosterone several months after birds have stopped singing leads to a rapid recurrence of song performance.
source: Re-treatment with testosterone several months after birds have stopped singing, leads to a rapid recurrence of song performance with song features that strongly resemble those after the first treatment.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figures 2-4.

claim: Song features after re-treatment strongly resemble those after the first treatment.
source: Re-treatment with testosterone several months after birds have stopped singing, leads to a rapid recurrence of song performance with song features that strongly resemble those after the first treatment.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figure 4.

claim: Once developed, vocal motor memories are retained for an extended period of time.
source: We propose that once developed, vocal motor memories are retained for an extended period of time, enabling adult animals to recover song performance quickly at a later time, a process termed 'savings' (Ebbinghaus, 2013).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings with reference to the concept of savings.

claim: Neurons in HVC irreversibly lose a significant number of dendritic spines during the initial testosterone-induced development of vocal skills.
source: We further demonstrate that neurons in the songbird's premotor nucleus HVC (proper name), a central nucleus in the brain circuitry that controls song production (Nottebohm et al., 1976), irreversibly loses a significant number of dendritic spines during the initial testosterone-induced development of vocal skills.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figure 5.

claim: HVC is a central nucleus in the brain circuitry that controls song production.
source: We further demonstrate that neurons in the songbird's premotor nucleus HVC (proper name), a central nucleus in the brain circuitry that controls song production (Nottebohm et al., 1976)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Nottebohm et al., 1976.

claim: The state of reduced spine density in HVC is maintained over long periods in which testosterone levels are low and vocal skills are not used.
source: This state of reduced spine density is subsequently maintained over long periods in which testosterone levels are low and vocal skills are not used.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figure 5 showing maintained low spine density in T1- group.

claim: The lasting synaptic pruning could play an important role in the formation of vocal skill savings.
source: The observed lasting synaptic pruning could play an important role in the formation of vocal skill savings, enabling birds to rapidly re-acquire song performance within a restricted time period.
evidence: This is an interpretation connecting the anatomical findings to the behavioral observations.

claim: The entire song ontogeny was recorded in acoustically separated animals, totaling 5.6 ± 0.6 million song syllables per bird.
source: To study the development of vocal skills in adult female canaries we recorded and analyzed the entire song ontogeny in acoustically separated animals (5.6 ± 0.6 million song syllables per bird)
evidence: This describes the experimental data collection.

claim: No songs were observed prior to testosterone treatment.
source: Whereas no songs were observed prior to treatment, the systemic application of testosterone (T1+) stimulated birds to start singing their first songs after three days (3.22 ± 0.46 days).
evidence: This is an experimental observation.

claim: The systemic application of testosterone stimulated birds to start singing their first songs after three days (3.22 ± 0.46 days).
source: Whereas no songs were observed prior to treatment, the systemic application of testosterone (T1+) stimulated birds to start singing their first songs after three days (3.22 ± 0.46 days).
evidence: This is an experimental observation with quantitative data.

claim: The phases of female song development were similar to those previously reported for male canaries.
source: The phases of female song development were similar to those previously reported for male canaries (Figure 1) (Nottebohm et al., 1986; Mori et al., 2018; Weichel et al., 1986).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and citations to previous studies.

claim: Female canary songs had relatively small syllable repertoires (6.2 ± 1.1 syllable types).
source: Although structurally similar to male canary songs, female songs had relatively small syllable repertoires (6.2 ± 1.1 syllable types), consistent with previous reports (Vallet et al., 1996; Fusani et al., 2003; Hartog et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by quantitative data and consistent with cited literature.

claim: Withdrawal of testosterone completely abolished singing behavior in approximately three days (3.14 ± 0.63 days).
source: To investigate the birds' abilities to re-acquire song performance after a period without vocal practice we withdrew testosterone (T1-) from the animals, completely abolishing singing behavior in approximately three days (3.14 ± 0.63 days).
evidence: This is an experimental observation with quantitative data.

claim: After 2½ months of no song production, birds were treated for a second time with testosterone, inducing song output after three days (3.14 ± 0.74 days).
source: After 2½ months of no song production birds were treated for a second time with testosterone (T2+), inducing song output after three days (3.14 ± 0.74 days).
evidence: This is an experimental observation with quantitative data.

claim: No subsongs were observed after the second testosterone treatment.
source: No subsongs were observed after the second testosterone treatment, and all birds were able to produce plastic songs from the first day of singing.
evidence: This is an experimental observation.

claim: All birds were able to produce plastic songs from the first day of singing after the second testosterone treatment.
source: No subsongs were observed after the second testosterone treatment, and all birds were able to produce plastic songs from the first day of singing.
evidence: This is an experimental observation.

claim: Syllable repetition rate has been strongly associated with individual performance.
source: Particularly the speed at which subsequent syllables are repeated, the syllable repetition rate (SR), has been strongly associated with individual performance (Podos, 1997; Podos, 1996)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Podos, 1997 and Podos, 1996.

claim: Syllable repetition rate has been shown to increase the attractiveness of the song to conspecifics.
source: and has been shown to increase the attractiveness of the song to conspecifics (Vallet et al., 1998; Vallet and Kreutzer, 1995)
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: During the first two weeks of testosterone-induced female song development, all syllables were typically produced at a similar rate (SR: 10.3 ± 1.3 Hz).
source: We observed that during the first two weeks of testosterone-induced female song development, all syllables were typically produced at a similar rate (SR: 10.3 ± 1.3 Hz).
evidence: This is an experimental observation with quantitative data.

claim: Once crystallized, syllables could be distinguished as fast syllables (SR: 21.7 ± 1.0 Hz), medium-speed syllables (SR: 11.9 ± 1.1 Hz), and slow syllables (SR: 4.9 ± 0.7 Hz).
source: Once crystallized, syllables could be distinguished as fast syllables (SR: 21.7 ± 1.0 Hz), medium-speed syllables (SR: 11.9 ± 1.1 Hz), and slow syllables (SR: 4.9 ± 0.7 Hz).
evidence: This is an experimental observation with quantitative data.

claim: The observed range of syllable rates was similar to what has previously been reported for wild-living male canaries.
source: The observed range of syllable rates was similar to what has previously been reported for wild-living male canaries (Leitner et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a comparison to cited literature.

claim: Syllable repetition rates gradually developed and stabilized over the course of 160 ± 8 days during the first testosterone treatment.
source: While syllable repetition rates gradually developed and stabilized over the course of 160 ± 8 days during the first testosterone treatment, stable rates were obtained more than seven times faster, within 22 ± 2 days, during the second treatment (Figure 2D; paired t-test: p<0.001).
evidence: This is an experimental finding with quantitative data and statistical analysis, shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Stable syllable repetition rates were obtained more than seven times faster during the second treatment, within 22 ± 2 days.
source: While syllable repetition rates gradually developed and stabilized over the course of 160 ± 8 days during the first testosterone treatment, stable rates were obtained more than seven times faster, within 22 ± 2 days, during the second treatment (Figure 2D; paired t-test: p<0.001).
evidence: This is an experimental finding with quantitative data and statistical analysis, shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The maximum daily increase in similarity (dmax) was significantly higher during song re-development than during initial song development.
source: In addition the maximum daily increase in similarity (dmax) was also significantly higher during song re-development than during initial song development (Figure 2E; dmax: 0.021 ± 0.005 for T1+, and 0.078 ± 0.012 for T2+; paired t-test: p<0.05)
evidence: This is an experimental finding with quantitative data and statistical analysis, shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Syllable durations developed slowly during the initial song acquisition, reaching stable values after 153 ± 19 days.
source: Syllable durations developed slowly during the initial song acquisition (T1+), reaching stable values after 153 ± 19 days, while pause durations stabilized in 82 ± 13 days (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an experimental finding with quantitative data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Pause durations stabilized in 82 ± 13 days during initial song acquisition.
source: Syllable durations developed slowly during the initial song acquisition (T1+), reaching stable values after 153 ± 19 days, while pause durations stabilized in 82 ± 13 days (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an experimental finding with quantitative data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Both temporal features re-emerged more quickly during song re-acquisition than during the first song developmental phase.
source: Both temporal features re-emerged more quickly during song re-acquisition (T2+) than during the first song developmental phase (duration: 4.8 ± 1.3 days; paired t-test: p<0.001; pause: 10.7 ± 2.2 days; paired t-test: p<0.01; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an experimental finding with quantitative data and statistical analysis shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Spectral features were more quickly established during song re-acquisition than during the initial song development.
source: Similar to temporal song features, spectral features were more quickly established during song re-acquisition (T2+) than during the initial song development (T1+) (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data in Figure 3 and supplementary figures.

claim: All spectral features developed gradually over more than 110 days before reaching stable values.
source: All spectral features developed gradually over more than 110 days before reaching stable values.
evidence: This is an experimental observation.

claim: Testosterone-induced song re-acquisition led to a rapid stabilization of spectral patterns within 16 days.
source: After a period in which the birds did not produce any song, testosterone-induced song re-acquisition led to a rapid stabilization of spectral patterns within 16 days (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1; paired t test: p<0.01).
evidence: This is an experimental finding with quantitative data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Syllable durations did not show any deterioration in the period that birds did not sing.
source: Of the studied temporal song parameters, syllable durations did not show any deterioration in the period that birds did not sing (T1-) and thus also did not need to be re-acquired (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C; Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Both the syllable rate and the pause duration between syllables deteriorated when birds stopped singing.
source: Both the syllable rate and the pause duration between syllables did deteriorate however, and a short phase of re-development was required to recover the originally developed patterns (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–F, Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 2 and supplementary figures.

claim: The FM and AM patterns deteriorated when birds stopped singing but were re-acquired during a short developmental phase after a 2nd testosterone treatment.
source: Of the spectral syllable features that were studied, the FM and AM patterns deteriorated when birds stopped singing (T1-), but were re-acquired during a short developmental phase after a 2nd testosterone treatment (T2+) (Figure 3A–C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A & B).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 3 and supplementary figures.

claim: BW, MF, and E did not need to be re-acquired, but maintained strong similarities with the initial acoustic patterns despite the absence of song production.
source: BW, MF, and E did not need to be re-acquired, but maintained strong similarities with the initial acoustic patterns despite the absence of song production in the intermittent period (T1-) (Figure 3D–F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–I, Figure 3—figure supplement 2C–E).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 3 and supplementary figures.

claim: The songs that reappeared during the second testosterone treatment were strikingly similar to those that developed after the first treatment.
source: The songs that reappeared during the second testosterone treatment were strikingly similar to those that developed after the first treatment (Figure 4).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 4.

claim: Visual inspection of the song spectrograms revealed no differences in syllable repertoire when comparing crystallized songs during the first and second testosterone treatment.
source: Visual inspection of the song spectrograms revealed no differences in syllable repertoire when comparing crystallized songs during the first and second testosterone treatment (Figure 4A & B; 6.2 ± 1.1 syllable types for both treatments).
evidence: This is an experimental observation with quantitative data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Both temporal and spectral song features demonstrated a strong similarity in their distribution patterns between subsequent testosterone treatments, with correlation coefficients above 0.82 for all studied song features.
source: In addition both temporal and spectral song features demonstrated a strong similarity in their distribution patterns between subsequent testosterone treatments (T1xT2), with correlation coefficients above 0.82 for all studied song features (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is an experimental finding with quantitative data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The mean Euclidean distances between syllables of the same type across the 1st and 2nd testosterone treatment were not different from the Euclidean distances between syllables from subsequent days during the 1st testosterone treatment.
source: The mean Euclidean distances between syllables of the same type across the 1st and 2nd testosterone treatment (T1xT2) were not different from the Euclidean distances between syllables from subsequent days during the 1st testosterone treatment (T1xT1: d = 0.73 ± 0.04, T1xT2: d = 0.76 ± 0.06; Tukey's HSD: p=0.99).
evidence: This is an experimental finding with quantitative data and statistical analysis.

claim: The mean Euclidean distances between syllables of different types across the two treatment periods were significantly larger than those between syllables of the same type.
source: The mean Euclidean distances between syllables of different types across the two treatment periods were significantly larger than those between syllables of the same type (T1xT2ext: d = 2.12 ± 0.23; Tukey's HSD: p<0.001).
evidence: This is an experimental finding with quantitative data and statistical analysis.

claim: On average only 8.7% of all possible phrase transitions were used in the songs.
source: Because the syllable repertoire is relatively small in testosterone treated female canaries, the number of possible phrase transitions is also small. Nevertheless, on average only 8.7% of all possible phrase transitions were used in the songs.
evidence: This is an experimental observation with quantitative data.

claim: The percentage of phrase transitions that made up the songs during the 1st and 2nd testosterone treatments were not different.
source: The percentage of phrase transitions that made up the songs during the 1st and 2nd testosterone treatments were not different (T1+: 9.2 ± 4.5%; T2+: 8.3 ± 4.2%; paired t-test: p=0.59)
evidence: This is an experimental finding with quantitative data and statistical analysis.

claim: The linearity, consistency, and entropy of song phrase transitions did not differ significantly between the songs from the 1st and 2nd treatment periods.
source: The linearity, consistency, and entropy of song phrase transitions did not differ significantly between the songs from the 1st and 2nd treatment periods (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is an experimental finding shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Motor learning and memory are generally considered to rely on the maturation and consolidation of the synaptic connections within the neural circuitry that drives the behavior in question.
source: Motor learning and memory are generally considered to rely on the maturation and consolidation of the synaptic connections within the neural circuitry that drives the behavior in question (Changeux and Danchin, 1976; Yu and Zuo, 2011; Hoshiba et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Excitatory projection neurons in the HVC of testosterone-treated, singing female canaries displayed a more than 30% reduction in dendritic spine density compared to untreated, non-singing control birds.
source: Excitatory projection neurons in the HVC of testosterone-treated, singing female canaries displayed a more than 30% reduction in dendritic spine density compared to untreated, non-singing control birds (C: 0.95 µm−1, T1+: 0.64 µm−1; Dunnett's test: p<0.01)
evidence: This is an experimental finding with quantitative data and statistical analysis.

claim: Spine densities remained significantly lower in birds that stopped singing for 2.5 months after testosterone removal compared to non-singing control birds.
source: Compared to non-singing control birds, spine densities remained significantly lower in birds that stopped singing for 2.5 months after testosterone removal (C: 0.95 µm−1, T1-: 0.69 µm−1; Dunnett's test: p<0.01).
evidence: This is an experimental finding with quantitative data and statistical analysis.

claim: No changes in dendritic spine densities in RA were observed across the different experimental periods.
source: In contrast, we did not observe any changes in dendritic spine densities in RA across the different experimental periods (Figure 5C; ANOVA: p=0.857).
evidence: This is an experimental finding with statistical analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: A marked shift in the distribution of dendrites from more densely-spined dendrites in control birds towards less densely-spined dendrites in the testosterone treatment and removal groups was observed.
source: We observed a marked shift in the distribution of dendrites from more densely-spined dendrites in control birds towards less densely-spined dendrites in the testosterone treatment (T1+) and removal groups (T1-), reflecting a global decrease in spine density.
evidence: This is an experimental observation.

claim: The strongest reduction was detected in the range of dendrites with more than 0.8 spines per µm, which halved in number in both testosterone-treated, singing birds and testosterone-removed, non-singing birds compared to non-singing controls.
source: The strongest reduction was detected in the range of dendrites with more than 0.8 spines per µm, which halved in number in both testosterone-treated, singing birds (T1+), and testosterone-removed, non-singing birds (T1-) compared to non-singing controls (C: 0.64 ± 0.06, T1+: 0.28 ± 0.05, T1-: 0.33 ± 0.06; ANOVA: p<0.01).
evidence: This is an experimental finding with quantitative data and statistical analysis.

claim: The total density of both spinous and aspinous neurites in HVC did not significantly differ between the treatment groups.
source: The total density of both spinous and aspinous neurites in HVC did not significantly differ between the treatment groups (ANOVA: p>0.36)
evidence: This is an experimental finding with statistical analysis.

claim: Changes in dendrite densities were not caused by specific cell death.
source: The total density of both spinous and aspinous neurites in HVC did not significantly differ between the treatment groups (ANOVA: p>0.36), suggesting that changes in dendrite densities were not caused by specific cell death.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that total neurite density did not change.

claim: The initial development of specialized motor skills can be a lengthy process.
source: Using this model, we show that while the initial development of specialized motor skills can be a lengthy process, motor performance can quickly be re-acquired at a later time, even after extended periods of non-use (Figure 2 and 3).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Motor performance can quickly be re-acquired at a later time, even after extended periods of non-use.
source: Using this model, we show that while the initial development of specialized motor skills can be a lengthy process, motor performance can quickly be re-acquired at a later time, even after extended periods of non-use (Figure 2 and 3).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Acquiring a motor skill for the first time follows a different developmental trajectory than re-acquiring the same skill at a later time.
source: The accelerated song re-acquisition observed in this study indicates that acquiring a motor skill for the first time follows a different developmental trajectory than re-acquiring the same skill at a later time.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Birds skip the subsong phase of song development when re-acquiring their songs.
source: This is both evident from the accelerated consolidation of song performance during song re-development (Figure 2 and 3), and the observation that birds skip the subsong phase of song development when re-acquiring their songs.
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Songbirds have the ability to retain previously developed singing skills through a process of selective pruning of the neural circuitry.
source: Our data further suggest that songbirds have the ability to retain previously developed singing skills through a process of selective pruning of the neural circuitry (Figure 5)
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings shown in Figure 5.

claim: Song features that required a phase of re-development to be optimized seem primarily associated with motor constraints in syrinx function.
source: Interestingly, those song features that required a phase of re-development to be optimized seem primarily associated with motor constraints in syrinx function (Podos, 1997; Geberzahn and Aubin, 2014).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings with reference to cited literature.

claim: Online modulation of frequency and amplitude requires active contractile modulation of syringeal muscles.
source: Online modulation of frequency and amplitude requires active contractile modulation of syringeal muscles (Goller and Suthers, 1996; Elemans et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Syllable repetition and the inter-syllabic interval depend on how rapidly syringeal abductor and adductor muscles can open and close the syringeal aperture.
source: Syllable repetition and the inter-syllabic interval also depend on how rapidly syringeal abductor and adductor muscles can open and close the syringeal aperture.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about vocal production mechanisms.

claim: The upper vocal tract may act as a tunable acoustic filter of the sounds produced by the syrinx.
source: The upper vocal tract may act as a tunable acoustic filter of the sounds produced by the syrinx (Nowicki, 1987; Beckers et al., 2003; Riede et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The upper vocal tract may play a more important role in establishing the bandwidth, entropy and mean frequency of song syllables.
source: and play a more important role in establishing the bandwidth, entropy and mean frequency of song syllables.
evidence: This is an inference based on the role of the vocal tract as an acoustic filter.

claim: Song parameters linked to vocal tract modulation may be preserved after birds stopped singing.
source: Thus song parameters linked to vocal tract modulation may be preserved after birds stopped singing, while song parameters linked to contraction speed of syringeal muscles appear to deteriorate.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Song parameters linked to contraction speed of syringeal muscles appear to deteriorate after birds stopped singing.
source: Thus song parameters linked to vocal tract modulation may be preserved after birds stopped singing, while song parameters linked to contraction speed of syringeal muscles appear to deteriorate.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Male canaries are known to annually re-organize their songs, even when deafened.
source: Whereas male canaries are known to annually re-organize their songs, even when deafened (Mori et al., 2018), no such modifications were observed in our study.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mori et al., 2018.

claim: No song modifications were observed in the female canaries in this study.
source: Whereas male canaries are known to annually re-organize their songs, even when deafened (Mori et al., 2018), no such modifications were observed in our study.
evidence: This is an experimental observation.

claim: The emerging song patterns in acoustically separated female canaries are either for a large part innate or are limited to a memorized collection of syllable types that they heard earlier in life.
source: Considering that the female canaries in our study were acoustically separated during the testosterone-induced development of song suggests that the emerging song patterns are either for a large part innate (Mori et al., 2018; Gardner et al., 2005), or are limited to a memorized collection of syllable types that they heard earlier in life (Belzner et al., 2009; Marler and Peters, 1981; Marler and Peters, 1982b; Prather et al., 2010; Kiefer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental conditions with reference to cited literature.

claim: The initial song acquisition may rely on an innate or memorized auditory template.
source: The initial song acquisition may thus rely on an innate or memorized auditory template, while the accelerated song re-acquisition may be driven by a motor memory trace of what the birds learned to produce during the first song acquisition phase.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: The accelerated song re-acquisition may be driven by a motor memory trace of what the birds learned to produce during the first song acquisition phase.
source: The initial song acquisition may thus rely on an innate or memorized auditory template, while the accelerated song re-acquisition may be driven by a motor memory trace of what the birds learned to produce during the first song acquisition phase.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: During juvenile brain development in humans, mammals, and birds, synaptic connections are initially overproduced, followed by protracted, activity-dependent synapse elimination during puberty.
source: During juvenile brain development in humans, mammals, and birds, synaptic connections are initially overproduced, followed by protracted, activity-dependent synapse elimination during puberty (Huttenlocher, 1990; Petanjek et al., 2011; Rakic et al., 1986; Zuo et al., 2005; Nixdorf-Bergweiler et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: By selectively stabilizing functional synapses while pruning away inactive synapses, brain circuits are thought to reduce neuronal plasticity, consolidating newly learned information and reducing unnecessary redundancy.
source: By selectively stabilizing functional synapses while pruning away inactive synapses, brain circuits are thought to reduce neuronal plasticity, consolidating newly learned information and reducing unnecessary redundancy (Changeux and Danchin, 1976).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Changeux and Danchin, 1976.

claim: The lasting spine pruning observed in HVC could reflect a structural modification facilitating the long-term memorization of vocal patterns.
source: The lasting spine pruning observed in the forebrain song control area HVC (Figure 5) could reflect such a structural modification facilitating the long-term memorization of vocal patterns.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings shown in Figure 5.

claim: Optical imaging studies have demonstrated a rapid accumulation and stabilization of neuronal dendritic spines in HVC during developmental song learning in zebra finches.
source: Optical imaging studies have demonstrated a rapid accumulation and stabilization of neuronal dendritic spines in HVC during developmental song learning in zebra finches (Roberts et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Roberts et al., 2010.

claim: In the mouse cortex, morphological modifications to dendritic spines have been observed that lasted well beyond the learning experience that caused the spine modifications.
source: In the mouse cortex, morphological modifications to dendritic spines have been observed that lasted well beyond the learning experience that caused the spine modifications (Hofer et al., 2006; Yang et al., 2009; Xu et al., 2009; Hofer et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The large majority of dendritic spines in the mammalian brain are stably maintained in adulthood.
source: Despite such learning-related circuit modifications, the large majority of dendritic spines in the mammalian brain are stably maintained in adulthood (Petanjek et al., 2011; Rakic et al., 1986; Zuo et al., 2005; Yang et al., 2009; Xu et al., 2009; Grutzendler et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: A strong spine reduction was observed in fully adult birds.
source: In contrast we observed a strong spine reduction in fully adult birds (Figure 5)
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 5.

claim: The observed synaptic pruning in the adult canary HVC during song acquisition may reflect a developmentally delayed, activity-dependent consolidation of the neural motor circuitry.
source: suggesting that the observed synaptic pruning in the adult canary HVC during song acquisition may reflect a developmentally delayed, activity-dependent consolidation of the neural motor circuitry.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Singing prevention during juvenile development can avert developmental spine pruning in the robust motor nucleus of the arcopallium (RA) in zebra finches.
source: A recent study in zebra finches has shown that singing prevention during juvenile development can also avert developmental spine pruning in the robust motor nucleus of the arcopallium (RA) (Hayase et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hayase et al., 2018.

claim: Auditory input during sensorimotor learning may play an important role in circuit consolidation.
source: In addition, auditory input during sensorimotor learning may play an important role in circuit consolidation, and auditory deprivation has been shown to delay the natural juvenile maturation of HVC in zebra finches (Huang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Huang et al., 2018.

claim: Auditory deprivation has been shown to delay the natural juvenile maturation of HVC in zebra finches.
source: In addition, auditory input during sensorimotor learning may play an important role in circuit consolidation, and auditory deprivation has been shown to delay the natural juvenile maturation of HVC in zebra finches (Huang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Huang et al., 2018.

claim: No delayed synaptic pruning in RA was observed upon song acquisition in adult female canaries.
source: but we did not observe delayed synaptic pruning in RA upon song acquisition in adult female canaries (Figure 5C)
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The time-window for large-scale spine pruning in RA may be more limited than in HVC.
source: suggesting that the time-window for large-scale spine pruning in RA may be more limited than in HVC.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that RA did not show delayed pruning while HVC did.

claim: The developmentally delayed maturation of HVC is consistent with the observation that testosterone-induced development of song performance in adult female canaries follows a juvenile male-like developmental trajectory.
source: The developmentally delayed maturation of HVC (Figure 5B) is consistent with our observation that the delayed, testosterone-induced development of song performance in adult female canaries follows a juvenile male-like developmental trajectory (Figure 1).
evidence: This is an interpretation connecting the anatomical and behavioral findings shown in Figures 1 and 5.

claim: In the absence of singing behavior, parts of the vocal motor circuit may remain plastic in adult female canaries, only consolidating once neural activity within the circuitry increases to drive testosterone-induced song output.
source: Thus, in the absence of singing behavior, parts of the vocal motor circuit may remain plastic in adult female canaries, only consolidating once neural activity within the circuitry increases to drive testosterone-induced song output.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Testosterone-induced song development in adult female canaries has previously been associated with changes in other neural attributes in HVC including an increase in volume, neuron numbers, increased vascularization, and changes in cellular structure.
source: Testosterone-induced song development in adult female canaries has previously been associated with changes in other neural attributes in HVC as well, including an increase in volume, neuron numbers (but not densities), increased vascularization, and changes in cellular structure (Vellema et al., 2014; Hartog et al., 2009; Gahr and Garcia-Segura, 1996; Nottebohm, 1980; Rasika et al., 1994; Louissaint et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Many of the observed modifications to the song system follow an annually changing pattern in seasonally breeding male songbirds.
source: Many of the observed modifications to the song system follow an annually changing pattern in seasonally breeding male songbirds (Nottebohm et al., 1986; Smith et al., 1997; Nottebohm, 1981; Kirn et al., 1994)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Withdrawing testosterone from male Gambel's white-crowned sparrows resulted in a rapid regression in HVC size, neuron number, and neuron size.
source: In addition, withdrawing testosterone from male Gambel's white-crowned sparrows, another well-studied seasonal singer, resulted in a rapid regression in HVC size, neuron number, and neuron size (Thompson et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Thompson et al., 2007.

claim: The lasting synaptic pruning observed in HVC is the first report of a song-related modification to the adult songbird brain that persists after the behavior itself is no longer expressed.
source: The lasting synaptic pruning that we observed in HVC is to our knowledge the first report of a song-related modification to the adult songbird brain that persists after the behavior itself is no longer expressed.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the finding based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: HVC is at a central position between the motor circuitry that controls song output and a forebrain-basal ganglia circuit.
source: HVC is at a central position between the motor circuitry that controls song output and a forebrain-basal ganglia circuit, analogous to the mammalian cortico-basal ganglia (CBG) circuit, which feeds back on the motor circuitry for song production (Brainard and Doupe, 2013; Nottebohm et al., 1976).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Firing patterns in HVC neurons that project to RA are closely associated with millisecond precision of syllable timing.
source: Firing patterns in HVC neurons that project to RA are closely associated with millisecond precision of syllable timing (Yu and Margoliash, 1996; Hahnloser et al., 2002; Amador et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: HVC is directly involved in maintaining time-related features of song performance.
source: suggesting that HVC is directly involved in maintaining time-related features of song performance.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited literature about HVC neuron firing patterns.

claim: Burst patterns in RA neurons are more closely associated with intrasyllabic structure.
source: Burst patterns in RA neurons on the other hand are more closely associated with intrasyllabic structure (Yu and Margoliash, 1996; Chi and Margoliash, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Slowing down brain processes by local cooling of HVC has been shown to change the intrasyllabic structure.
source: However, slowing down brain processes by local cooling of HVC has also been shown to change the intrasyllabic structure (Long and Fee, 2008; Alonso et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Both HVC and RA activity play a role in maintaining the fine temporal structure within syllables.
source: indicating that both HVC and RA activity play a role in maintaining the fine temporal structure within syllables.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited literature.

claim: The acquisition of song syllables in zebra finches is accompanied by increased timing accuracy of inhibitory neural firing within the HVC microcircuitry.
source: The acquisition of song syllables in zebra finches is accompanied by increased timing accuracy of inhibitory neural firing within the HVC microcircuitry, suggesting that precisely-timed inhibition may play an important role in shaping song-related premotor sequences (Kosche et al., 2015; Vallentin et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Precisely-timed inhibition may play an important role in shaping song-related premotor sequences.
source: The acquisition of song syllables in zebra finches is accompanied by increased timing accuracy of inhibitory neural firing within the HVC microcircuitry, suggesting that precisely-timed inhibition may play an important role in shaping song-related premotor sequences (Kosche et al., 2015; Vallentin et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on cited literature.

claim: The lasting synaptic reorganization in HVC during song acquisition may be guided by inhibitory activity and provide a neural scaffold for both intra and intersyllabic timing.
source: The lasting synaptic reorganization in HVC during song acquisition may be guided by such inhibitory activity and provide a neural scaffold for both intra and intersyllabic timing.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: RA-projecting HVC neurons are continuously replaced in the adult songbird brain.
source: RA-projecting HVC neurons are continuously replaced in the adult songbird brain (Alvarez-Buylla et al., 1990)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Alvarez-Buylla et al., 1990.

claim: A permanently maintained HVC network may guide dynamically changing circuits in HVC and RA during subsequent periods of singing.
source: A permanently maintained HVC network may guide dynamically changing circuits in HVC and RA during subsequent periods of singing, quickly driving song features towards previously acquired patterns.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Neurons from HVC that project to the avian basal ganglia Area X are not replaced in adulthood.
source: Neurons from HVC that project to the avian basal ganglia Area X are not replaced in adulthood, providing a permanent subpopulation of HVC neurons (Gahr, 1990; Alvarez-Buylla et al., 1988).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The strongest reduction of 50% was observed in the number of densely-spined dendrites in HVC after birds developed song.
source: Although we could not specifically distinguish between neuron types in our study, we observed the strongest reduction of 50% in the number of densely-spined dendrites in HVC after birds developed song.
evidence: This is an experimental observation.

claim: HVC neurons that project to Area X predominantly consist of neurons with densely-spined dendrites.
source: Previous studies have shown that those HVC neurons that project to Area X predominantly consist of neurons with densely-spined dendrites (Kornfeld et al., 2017; Nixdorf et al., 1989; Kubota and Taniguchi, 1998; Benton et al., 1998; Mooney, 2000; Mooney and Prather, 2005; Fortune and Margoliash, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The observed synaptic pruning may be related to a major reorganization within the HVC to Area X connection.
source: Thus our observed synaptic pruning may be related to a major reorganization within the HVC to Area X connection, a reorganization that could reflect the long-term memorization of vocal skills.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: CBG-like circuits have been strongly implicated in the learning and long-term retention of motor skills in humans.
source: CBG-like circuits have been strongly implicated in the learning and long-term retention of motor skills in humans (Albouy et al., 2008; Debas et al., 2010; Lehéricy et al., 2006; Poldrack et al., 2005; Coynel et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: CBG-like circuits have been strongly implicated in the learning and long-term retention of motor skills in mammals.
source: mammals (Barnes et al., 2005; Pasupathy and Miller, 2005; Sheth et al., 2011; Yin et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: CBG-like circuits have been strongly implicated in the learning and long-term retention of motor skills in birds.
source: and birds (Bottjer et al., 1984; Scharff and Nottebohm, 1991; Brainard and Doupe, 2000; Kao et al., 2005; Olveczky et al., 2005; Aronov et al., 2008; Sober and Brainard, 2009; Andalman and Fee, 2009; Ölveczky et al., 2011; Charlesworth et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Vocal exploration is driven by activity in the avian CBG circuit.
source: Vocal exploration is driven by activity in the avian CBG circuit (Kao et al., 2005)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kao et al., 2005.

claim: The avian CBG circuit may guide synaptic modifications in plastic motor circuits.
source: which may guide synaptic modifications in plastic motor circuits (Mehaffey and Doupe, 2015), even in adulthood.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mehaffey and Doupe, 2015.

claim: Selective elimination of X-projecting HVC neurons did not appear to alter the song structure of adult zebra finches.
source: Although selective elimination of X-projecting HVC neurons did not appear to alter the song structure of adult zebra finches (Scharff et al., 2000)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Scharff et al., 2000.

claim: Altered expression of FoxP2 in Area X of adult male zebra finches has been associated with changes in vocal performance.
source: altered expression of FoxP2 in Area X of adult male zebra finches has been associated with changes in vocal performance (Murugan et al., 2013; Thompson et al., 2013; Teramitsu and White, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Neurotoxic lesions in Area X lead to changes in singing tempo and syllable sequencing in adult zebra finches.
source: In addition neurotoxic lesions in Area X lead to changes in singing tempo and syllable sequencing in adult zebra finches (Kubikova et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kubikova et al., 2014.

claim: The HVC to Area X connection continues to play a role in the long-term maintenance of vocal sequences.
source: suggesting that the HVC to Area X connection continues to play a role in the long-term maintenance of vocal sequences.
evidence: This is an inference based on cited literature.

claim: Sex hormones may play an important role in the stabilization of synaptic connections during the development of motor skills.
source: The mechanisms behind learning-related, selective stabilization and elimination of dendritic spines remain largely unknown. Sex hormones may play an important role in the stabilization of such synaptic connections during the development of motor skills.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential mechanisms.

claim: Many of the brain areas that are involved in song learning and production express high numbers of androgen receptors.
source: Many of the brain areas that are involved in song learning and production express high numbers of androgen receptors (Arnold et al., 1976; Balthazart et al., 1992; Metzdorf et al., 1999; Nastiuk and Clayton, 1995; Gahr and Metzdorf, 1997)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: X-projecting HVC neurons express estrogen receptors that can be activated after conversion of testosterone into estradiol.
source: and X-projecting HVC neurons express estrogen receptors (Gahr, 1990) that can be activated after conversion of testosterone into estradiol.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gahr, 1990.

claim: Changes in neuronal dendritic growth and synaptic morphology in the songbird RA have been observed to accompany testosterone-induced song development in female canaries.
source: Furthermore, changes in neuronal dendritic growth and synaptic morphology in the songbird RA have been observed to accompany testosterone-induced song development in female canaries (DeVoogd and Nottebohm, 1981; Devoogd et al., 1985; Canady et al., 1988).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: 85% of the seasonally and testosterone upregulated genes in the canary HVC are related to neuron differentiation, axon, dendrite and synapse organization.
source: In addition, Frankl-Vilches et al. (Frankl-Vilches et al., 2015) recently observed that 85% of the seasonally and testosterone upregulated genes in the canary HVC are related to neuron differentiation, axon, dendrite and synapse organization.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Frankl-Vilches et al., 2015.

claim: In the brain of birds and mammals, sex hormones are known to upregulate the expression of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF).
source: In the brain of birds and mammals, sex hormones are known to upregulate the expression of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) (Dittrich et al., 1999; Rasika et al., 1999; Sohrabji et al., 1995)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: BDNF contributes to the stabilization of synapses through the interaction with tyrosine receptor kinase B (TrkB).
source: which in its turn contributes to the stabilization of synapses through the interaction with tyrosine receptor kinase B (TrkB) (Koleske, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Koleske, 2013.

claim: BDNF has been shown to be essential during testosterone-induced song development in female canaries.
source: Furthermore, BDNF has been shown to be essential during testosterone-induced song development in female canaries (Hartog et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hartog et al., 2009.

claim: BDNF provides a likely pathway by which sex hormones can consolidate motor skills by stabilizing synapses.
source: providing a likely pathway by which sex hormones can consolidate motor skills by stabilizing synapses.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited literature about BDNF function.

claim: Testosterone levels and song consolidation are tightly linked.
source: Testosterone levels and song consolidation are tightly linked, and it is difficult to determine if brain anatomical changes in our and other studies are caused by testosterone, singing activity or both.
evidence: This is a statement about the difficulty of separating effects in the experimental design.

claim: Local intracerebral testosterone implants close to nucleus RA did not cause anatomical changes in this androgen receptor-rich brain area.
source: Interestingly, local intracerebral testosterone implants close to nucleus RA did not cause anatomical changes in this androgen receptor-rich brain area (Brenowitz and Lent, 2002)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Brenowitz and Lent, 2002.

claim: Modifications in RA are driven by singing-related, activity-dependent input from HVC.
source: suggesting that modifications in RA are driven by singing-related, activity-dependent input from HVC.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited literature.

claim: The vocal circuitry demonstrated synaptic changes that persisted through several months in which testosterone levels were low and birds did not sing.
source: Whether or not testosterone, vocal practice, or both play a role in the observed synaptic pruning in HVC, the vocal circuitry demonstrated synaptic changes that persisted through several months in which testosterone levels were low and birds did not sing, potentially enabling the birds to quickly re-acquire their previously developed song patterns.
evidence: This is an experimental observation.

claim: Sex hormones can be regulated by both environmental and social factors.
source: Sex hormones can be regulated by both environmental and social factors (Goymann et al., 2007; Oliveira, 2004; Wingfield et al., 1990)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Lasting, hormone-driven synaptic pruning of related brain circuitries could form a basis for long-term memories, enabling a quick recovery of previously acquired skills.
source: Our study suggests that lasting, hormone-driven synaptic pruning of related brain circuitries could form a basis for such long-term memories, enabling a quick recovery of previously acquired skills.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: The ability to respond quickly to environmental and social cues through primed hormone-sensitive control mechanisms would constitute an important adaptation to ensure competitive proficiency and maximize reproductive success under environmental restrictions.
source: The ability to respond quickly to environmental and social cues through such primed hormone-sensitive control mechanisms would constitute an important adaptation to ensure competitive proficiency and maximize reproductive success under environmental restrictions.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the adaptive significance of the findings.

claim: The results obtained from this study may have implications not only across different animal groups, but may generally apply to different motor, sensory, and motivational systems that rely on a rapid recall of previously learned information.
source: The results obtained from this study may have implications not only across different animal groups, but may generally apply to different motor, sensory, and motivational systems that rely on a rapid recall of previously learned information.
